documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
         BEFORE THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

               Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC          Docket No. CP26-11-000

             REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF BENJAMIN M. PADGETT

Pursuant to section 19(a) of the Natural Gas Act, 15 U.S.C. § 717r(a), and Rule 713 of the
Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.713, Benjamin M. Padgett
respectfully requests rehearing of the Commission's Order Issuing Certificate, Columbia Gulf
Transmission, LLC, 197 FERC ¶ 61,031 (October 15, 2026), authorizing the Pulaski Project.

Mr. Padgett is a party to this proceeding (Order P 6 & n.11) and the owner of record of Tract
KY-LI-066.000, a 46.8-acre farm on Mahr Road, Waynesburg, Lincoln County, Kentucky,
operated as Full Circle Farms, a registered Red Gelbvieh seedstock cattle operation. The
certificated route crosses the farm and takes five of its nine permanent paddocks out of the
grazing rotation, including the farm's entire 10.9-acre winter pasture (Exhibit A).

Communications regarding this request should be directed to:

Benjamin M. Padgett
1391 Greenbrier Road
Waynesburg, KY 40489
(606) 303-4375
fullcirclefarmswaynesburg@gmail.com

                                STATEMENT OF ISSUES
Issue 1. Whether the Commission acted arbitrarily and capriciously by finding livestock and
groundwater impacts acceptable (Order PP 44-46) while failing to respond to the landowners'
argument that Columbia Gulf's commitment to provide frost-proof automated watering in all
affected paddocks is unenforceable as written, and by leaving that commitment, and any
coordination with livestock breeding operations, without specific terms, deadlines, or tract-
level verification; and whether the Commission should clarify that the EA § B.4.1 watering
commitment is binding under Appendix Condition 1 and Ordering Paragraph (A) and adopt
specific conditions to carry it out. See 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e); 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); Motor
Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

Issue 2. Whether the Commission's need finding (Order PP 14-15, 25) and its response to
concerns about data-center end use (P 54) are arbitrary and unsupported by substantial




                                         Page 1 of 16
 evidence, where the Commission relied solely on a precedent agreement with East Kentucky
Power Cooperative, declined to examine the generation facility the gas will serve, and relied
on the applicant's own statement that no data centers were identified, without inquiring into
East Kentucky's own public statements to the Kentucky Public Service Commission (Case No.
2025-00087) that the new Cooper Station capacity may serve data-center demand under
confidential large-load arrangements, and without weighing Kentucky's public policy on data-
center development, including Executive Order 2026-494. See 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e);
Certification of New Interstate Natural Gas Pipeline Facilities, 88 FERC ¶ 61,227 (1999);
Environmental Defense Fund v. FERC, 2 F.4th 953 (D.C. Cir. 2021).

Issue 3. Whether the Commission failed to engage in reasoned decision-making by
authorizing eminent domain against landowners on a need record whose true end-use demand
is shielded from them by the project shipper's confidentiality agreements with undisclosed
large-load customers, while declining to examine that demand (Order PP 14, 54). See 5 U.S.C.
§ 706(2)(A); Environmental Defense Fund v. FERC, 2 F.4th 953 (D.C. Cir. 2021).

Issue 4. Whether the Commission failed to adequately weigh the adverse effects of the project
on affected agricultural landowners, as the Certificate Policy Statement requires, including:
Columbia Gulf's failure to respond to landowners' documented operational needs (PP 23, 42);
the loss of five of nine paddocks and the entire winter pasture; disruption of USDA-NRCS
conservation practices under a 2026–2030 contract; herd-health effects of lost rotation;
disruption of food production; the permanent loss of the land's agricultural and future-use
potential; the order's reliance on studies of neighboring parcels rather than bisected host
parcels (P 24); reliance on eminent domain in place of good-faith agreement; and Kentucky's
policy, in House Bill 542 (2026), that agricultural value and improvements be counted in fair
market value. See Certification of New Interstate Natural Gas Pipeline Facilities, 88 FERC ¶
61,227 (1999); 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

Issue 5. Whether the Commission erred by issuing a certificate that allows construction on
agricultural land before the landowner's property rights have been acquired by agreement or
just compensation has been finally determined and paid, where the order disclaims any
authority over compensation (Order PP 42, 46) and certificate holders may obtain immediate
possession of land through federal court before compensation is decided. See U.S. Const.
amend. V; 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e), (h); East Tennessee Natural Gas Co. v. Sage, 361 F.3d 808 (4th
Cir. 2004).

ISSUE 1: THE LIVESTOCK WATER AND BREEDING COMMITMENTS MUST BE
                          ENFORCEABLE




                                         Page 2 of 16
 A. Mr. Padgett raised this issue first, and the record recognizes it. Mr. Padgett's January
16, 2026 comment (Accession No. 20260116-5008) explained that the route would cut the
farm's paddocks off from their water. The Environmental Assessment (Accession No.
20260622-3006, § B.4.1, p. 19) cites that comment and records Columbia Gulf's response: it
would either provide frost-proof automated watering systems in all affected paddocks before
ground disturbance, or an agreeable alternative mitigative solution with the landowner.

A-1. The landowners are already paying for water infrastructure, at substantial expense
partly cost-shared by NRCS, while Columbia Gulf stays silent. The Padgetts described the
farm's water needs in their July 28, 2026 counter-proposal and their August 2026 paperwork to
Columbia Gulf. Columbia Gulf said only that it was reviewing them. Knowing the pipeline
was coming, and with no substantive answer from Columbia Gulf, the Padgetts installed the
livestock waterers and fencing themselves, completing the work by September 30, 2026, under
a 2026–2030 Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP) contract with the USDA Natural
Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), and hired a fencing contractor to fence the entire
farm so hay fields can be converted to pasture. The family was forced to make that investment
now because the pipeline is coming, while Columbia Gulf has not said how or when it will
meet its own commitment. Columbia Gulf has not paid for them, acknowledged them, or
confirmed whether it will treat them as the "agreeable alternative mitigative solution"
described in the EA. Columbia Gulf has not said how or when it will meet the commitment on
this tract, despite written requests, and in the meantime the cost of water infrastructure has
fallen on the landowner. That is direct evidence that an unconditioned promise is not
mitigation.

B. The order restates the objection and never answers it. Paragraph 44 of the order recites
the landowners' argument that Columbia Gulf's watering commitment "is unenforceable and
that the EA does not identify specific details on the infrastructure affected, set enforceable pre-
construction milestones, or address the permanent loss of the water source." Paragraph 45 then
discusses groundwater depth, well testing, general livestock-movement procedures, and a 300-
yard breeding setback. It never addresses replacement water for paddocks the right-of-way
cuts off, and it never explains why the commitment needs no condition. None of the 16
environmental conditions in the Appendix mentions livestock, paddocks, pastures, or
agricultural water. Condition 1 requires Columbia Gulf generally to follow the mitigation
measures "identified in the environmental assessment," but the EA measure itself lets
Columbia Gulf choose between the watering systems and an undefined "agreeable
alternative," with no deadline, no specifics, and no requirement to show the Commission that
it was met on any tract. An agency that identifies a significant objection and then does not
respond to it has not engaged in reasoned decision-making. Mr. Padgett's own January 16,




                                            Page 3 of 16
 2026 comment, the source of this commitment in the EA, is not discussed anywhere in the
order.

C. The Commission itself treated the issue as unresolved, then accepted less. On July 27,
2026, Commission staff asked Columbia Gulf (Accession No. 20260727-3051) whether it
would coordinate with landowners around active livestock breeding operations within 500
yards of the project, and to update its plans for permanent replacement water in all affected
paddocks. The order (P 45) accepts Columbia Gulf's August 3, 2026 answer that it will
coordinate on a 300-yard setback — less than staff asked about — and imposes nothing at all
on the replacement water. The order also relies on Section III.F.3 of the Commission's Plan,
which requires only general procedures for livestock movement during construction, not
replacement water for paddocks permanently cut off from it. For a year-round calving herd, a
setback alone does not protect the cattle: cows are calving and being bred every month of the
year, so scheduling around them is not possible. The only way to keep this herd safely away
from construction is a confinement facility with its own water.

D. Relying on unenforceable mitigation is arbitrary. The order's finding that impacts on
livestock are acceptable depends on mitigation the certificate does not plainly require. If the
Commission believes Appendix Condition 1, or Ordering Paragraph (A), which authorizes the
project "as more fully described in the application and subsequent filings by the applicant,
including any commitments made therein," already binds Columbia Gulf to install the
watering systems before ground disturbance, it should say so expressly, so that the
commitment can be enforced through the Commission's compliance process. If it does not, it
should impose the condition.

E. The harm here is specific and severe. Full Circle Farms runs a year-round calving
registered Red Gelbvieh seedstock herd, currently 15 cows and 1 bull, on ground that can
carry about 25 cows. The route crosses paddocks 2, 3, 4, and 9, and construction also takes out
paddock 6, the wooded winter pasture, which the farm divides with temporary fencing into
additional paddocks during the grazing season (Exhibit A). That is five of nine permanent
paddocks, and every acre of winter pasture. The herd cannot be maintained on the four
paddocks that remain. Confinement with a dependable water supply is the only workable way
the operation survives construction and the years of pasture recovery that follow.

F. The fix is narrow and within the Commission's power. Andrew and Christopher Daniels,
landowners on this route, proposed condition language with fixed deadlines (Order P 44). The
Commission rejected their request for compensation (P 46) but never ruled on the conditions
themselves. Mr. Padgett asks the Commission to adopt conditions of that kind, set out in the
relief requested below.




                                          Page 4 of 16
   ISSUE 2: THE NEED FINDING RESTS ON DEMAND NO ONE HAS EXAMINED
A. The Commission must look past the contract to the actual need. A precedent agreement
is evidence of need, but it is not the end of the inquiry. In Environmental Defense Fund v.
FERC, the D.C. Circuit vacated a certificate because the Commission relied on a precedent
agreement with an affiliated shipper while failing to respond to evidence that raised real
questions about whether the project served genuine new demand. East Kentucky is not
affiliated with Columbia Gulf, but the principle applies: when the record raises questions
about what the capacity is actually for, the Commission must engage with them rather than
stop at the contract. The Certificate Policy Statement likewise requires the Commission to
weigh public benefits against the harm to landowners whose property will be taken.

B. The shipper is openly preparing to serve data centers, and says it cannot tell anyone
which ones. The order confirms the project's sole shipper is East Kentucky Power
Cooperative, which holds 100% of the 260,000 Dth/d capacity under a 20-year precedent
agreement to fuel a new gas-fired unit at Cooper Station (Order PP 1, 5, 14). That same
cooperative:

      obtained a special data-center tariff from the Kentucky Public Service Commission,
      approved October 30, 2025, for data centers using 15 megawatts or more, with added
      terms for those above 250 megawatts;
      as reported from its March 2026 testimony before the Kentucky Public Service
      Commission, said it had no data-center contract yet, but that data-center demand could
      be met with its existing generation and the new plants it plans to build, including the
      745-megawatt Pulaski County unit this pipeline will fuel;
      told the Kentucky Public Service Commission, in a March 16, 2026 response in Case
      No. 2025-00087, that its non-disclosure agreements with prospective large-load
      customers "preclude[] any public disclosure of potential data center projects prior to
      signing a 'special contract'" and "prevent[] the Company from disclosing any
      anonymized information about a proposed project, such as its size"; and
      serves the territory where, on October 13, 2026, Mason County approved a 40-year tax
      agreement for a hyperscale data-center campus reported to need up to 1.2 gigawatts of
      power.

Because these are public records of a state agency and a local government, some arising after
the order issued, Mr. Padgett asks the Commission to take official notice of them or, if
necessary, to reopen the record under Rule 716, 18 C.F.R. § 385.716, to receive them.




                                         Page 5 of 16
 C. The order looked away from the question. Paragraph 15 states that issues related to East
Kentucky's "plan to replace coal-fired generation with natural gas co-fired generation are
outside the scope of this proceeding" and that the Commission will "not second-guess" the
shipper's business decisions. Paragraph 54 answers data-center concerns only by noting that
Columbia Gulf's cumulative-impacts review identified "no planned data centers" within the
project's geographic scope. That is not an answer. A search radius drawn around a pipeline
says nothing about who will use the electricity a 745-megawatt power plant puts on the grid. A
data center does not need to sit beside the pipeline to run on Cooper Station's power; it only
needs to be on the system that plant supplies. The Commission relied on the applicant's own
search radius and did not inquire into the shipper's own public statements. Without examining
that evidence, the Commission cannot reasonably find that the public benefits of this project
outweigh taking farmland from landowners like the Padgetts.

D. Kentucky has made data-center demand a matter of public policy. The Commission
cannot treat it as invisible. Data-center development has become one of the most contested
land-use questions in Kentucky. On August 6, 2026, the Governor signed Executive Order
2026-494, which requires data-center developers to submit energy plans showing they will not
raise electric bills for families and existing businesses and to commit to transparency with the
public, and directs the Public Service Commission to keep utilities from passing data-center
costs on to other customers. Oldham and Nelson Counties have adopted data-center
moratoriums, and other local governments have refused data-center rezoning, in response to
public concern. Kentucky now asks data-center developers to prove they will not burden the
public's electric bills. No one has asked whether the landowners whose farms are condemned
for the fuel supply are carrying that burden instead. The Commission is the only body in a
position to ask, because it is the Commission's certificate that authorizes the taking.

E. Why it matters. Eminent domain under the Natural Gas Act is justified by public need. If a
meaningful share of the demand is private, single-customer load that is shielded from public
view, the balance the Commission struck is not supported by the record.

        ISSUE 3: LANDOWNERS WERE KEPT FROM TESTING THE NEED
A. The demand behind the need is hidden from the people losing their land. The shipper's
identity is public, but the demand that shipper is building to serve is not. East Kentucky has
told the Kentucky Public Service Commission that its non-disclosure agreements "preclude[]
any public disclosure of potential data center projects prior to signing a 'special contract'" and
prevent it from disclosing even "anonymized information about a proposed project, such as its
size" (Case No. 2025-00087, response dated March 16, 2026). The landowners whose property




                                            Page 6 of 16
 may be condemned therefore cannot learn how much of the new Cooper Station capacity, and
of this pipeline, exists to serve private data-center load rather than the cooperative's existing
members.

B. Secrecy at the state level, and no inquiry at the federal level. The end user's prospective
large-load customers are shielded by confidentiality at the state level, and the Commission
relied on the precedent agreement alone at the federal level (PP 14, 54). The result is that no
forum examines the demand that justifies taking private land, and no affected landowner can
test it.

C. That is not reasoned decision-making. An agency must examine the relevant data and
explain a rational connection between the facts and its choice. The landowners whose farms
will be condemned are the only parties in this proceeding who cannot see what their land is
being taken for. When the facts behind need are hidden from the parties most harmed, the
Commission's need finding cannot be meaningfully tested, and the balancing it performed is
not adequately explained.

D. The Commission can fix this without second-guessing the shipper. It need only require
East Kentucky, an intervenor in this proceeding (Order P 6), to state on the record whether any
portion of the contracted capacity is intended to serve data-center or other large-load
customers under confidential arrangements, filed publicly or, at a minimum, under a protective
agreement available to affected landowners, and then weigh that answer in its public-interest
balancing.

     ISSUE 4: THE HARM TO FARM FAMILIES WAS NOT FAIRLY WEIGHED
A. The order's landowner finding rests on the company's word. The Certificate Policy
Statement asks whether a project's benefits outweigh its adverse effects on landowners, and
treats reliance on eminent domain as a cost in that balance. The order finds that Columbia Gulf
"has taken appropriate steps to minimize adverse economic impacts on landowners" based on
Columbia Gulf's own statement that "it has been working with affected landowners" (P 23).
The order also states that "the Commission expects companies to engage in good faith
negotiations with landowners" (P 42). The record on this tract contradicts both premises.

B. Columbia Gulf has not responded to the farm's documented needs. The Padgetts
mailed Columbia Gulf a detailed counter-proposal on July 28, 2026, and sent further
paperwork that was delivered on August 8, 2026. Because no one signed for the delivery, the
Padgetts followed up by email, and Columbia Gulf confirmed that it had received the
paperwork and was reviewing it. They explained that the project takes five of nine permanent




                                           Page 7 of 16
 paddocks, including all of the winter pasture, out of a registered Red Gelbvieh seedstock
rotation and strands water on the wrong side of the line. Beyond that acknowledgment,
Columbia Gulf has given no substantive answer. A company that has not engaged with a
landowner's operational needs, yet now holds the power to condemn, has not earned the
weight the order gives its good-faith efforts.

C. The timing makes the harm worse. Cattle producers are carrying sharply higher input
costs for feed, fuel, fencing, and equipment. Losing more than half of the grazing rotation,
including all of the winter pasture, forces confinement feeding and new infrastructure at the
worst possible moment. It cuts the farm's income while the company offers no fair payment
for that loss, only for the strip of ground the easement covers. This is land that produces food.
The order weighs the pipeline's benefits but gives no weight to the lost income of the farm
families who feed people from this ground.

D. Food production is at stake. This farm produces beef, and other working farms along the
route also produce food. At a time when Kentucky and the nation are treating food security as
a priority, the order weighs none of the lost production from these working farms. The
disruption is not limited to one operation. It reaches every food-producing farm on the route,
through years of construction and pasture recovery. For Full Circle Farms, the financial cost of
confinement, feed, water infrastructure, and lost production is large, and it is not reflected
anywhere in the Commission's balancing of benefits and harms.

E. Paying for the strip is not paying for the loss. Columbia Gulf's offer compensates only
for the easement strip and temporary workspace. It pays nothing for the five paddocks and the
winter pasture taken out of the rotation, the water cut off from the herd, the confinement and
feed the operation now requires, or the permanent limits on what the rest of the farm can
become. With today's land values and input costs, an easement-only payment shifts the true
cost of this project onto the farm family. A pipeline company that can condemn has little
reason to offer more. The Commission should not approve the use of eminent domain on a
record that treats a strip payment as fair treatment of the landowner.

F. The harm has already started, and it will not end. Without the means to replace water
and feed the herd in confinement, Full Circle Farms will have to cut its production roughly in
half for those years. The farm cannot establish permanent pastures in the affected areas,
because the pipeline will tear them up. It still carries the annual fuel, labor, and seed costs on
that ground, with no help from anyone. The herd cannot grow now, because the farm knows
the line is coming and will not be able to support the number of cows the land could otherwise
carry. The pipeline changes the direction of the whole operation and its income. Yet the only




                                            Page 8 of 16
 offer is a bare easement payment, while the reduced earning capacity of the farm is permanent
and falls entirely on the farm family.

G. Federally cost-shared conservation work is in the pipeline's path. By September 30,
2026, the Padgetts completed new fencing and livestock watering under a 2026–2030
Conservation Stewardship Program contract with USDA-NRCS (Farm 1895, Tract 1996), and
NRCS has been informed of the pipeline route. The NRCS conservation plan for the farm's
32.4 acres of pasture includes exclusion and interior fencing, a livestock pipeline, frost-free
watering facilities, and heavy-use area protection in 2026; pasture and hay planting in 2027
and 2028; and prescribed grazing across all 32.4 acres in 2029. Those are the same years the
pipeline is to be built: Columbia Gulf has targeted an in-service date of February 1, 2029, and
the order requires the project to be in service within three years (Ordering Paragraph (C)(1)).
NRCS is to cost-share 50% of two of the watering facilities. The family paid the full cost of a
third waterer at the winter feeding area in the winter pasture (W3 on Exhibit A), and has hired
a fencing contractor to fence the entire farm so hay fields can be used as pasture while five of
nine paddocks are under construction at times no one can predict. The family is now finishing
fencing and a water station for a new bull lot as well. These practices are designed to be
maintained and used for the full contract term. Within that term, the pipeline will put five of
nine paddocks under construction and pasture recovery, disrupting the very practices one
federal agency has just helped pay for. The order does not mention NRCS conservation
practices on affected farms, how construction will avoid or restore them, or who bears the cost
if the landowner cannot meet contract requirements because of the pipeline. One federal
program should not be undone by another without any accounting for it.

H. Herd health suffers when rotation stops. Rotational grazing is how a cattle operation
breaks parasite cycles: animals move off contaminated ground before parasite loads build.
With five of nine paddocks under construction and the herd held in a smaller, more confined
area, the cattle will stand on the same ground day after day. That raises the risk of internal
parasites and of coccidiosis, a parasitic disease spread through manure-contaminated soil that
strikes calves hardest. In a year-round calving herd, there are always young calves exposed.
The farm will need ongoing preventive treatment, such as amprolium (Corid), and more
frequent parasite control for as long as rotation is disrupted. The order does not consider
animal health at all.

I. The land's future is being taken, not just a strip. A permanent pipeline easement through
the middle of the farm limits what the land can be used for after construction is over: future
homesites, subdivision for the next generation, new buildings, and changes to how the herd is
run. Those losses last for every future owner, and the order does not weigh them.




                                           Page 9 of 16
 J. Eminent domain is being used as leverage, not as a last resort. The Certificate Policy
Statement treats reliance on eminent domain as a cost to be minimized. Here, instead of
negotiating in good faith for the true value of the property and the real disruption to the farm,
Columbia Gulf can simply wait for its certificate and condemn. That leaves farm families,
already facing high input costs on every side, with a choice between accepting whatever the
company offers or paying to fight in federal court. The power to condemn has become the
company's bargaining power over the price.

K. Other energy developers must pay what the land is worth. Other energy projects across
rural Kentucky, such as utility-scale solar farms, have generally secured farmland through
leases and purchases negotiated with willing landowners, at prices both sides accept.
Columbia Gulf, a for-profit company earning a return on this project, holds a federal
certificate that frees it from that discipline. Farmland is being taken for a project on which a
private company will earn a return, while the landowners bear losses the company has not
offered to pay. The Commission should weigh that imbalance before allowing eminent domain
against agricultural land.

L. The order's property-value reasoning answers the wrong question. The order sets
property-value concerns aside because the effect is "difficult to separate" and valuation is
"inherently speculative" (P 24). The EA relied on a literature review (Wilde et al. 2012) of
properties near pipelines, which keep all of their land and use. Neither the order nor the EA
considers host parcels like this farm, which the pipeline cuts in two. The severance harm to a
working cattle farm is not speculative: it is five of nine paddocks out of service, including the
entire winter pasture, water stranded across the line, and a herd that cannot grow.

M. Kentucky has recognized exactly this harm. In 2026, Kentucky enacted House Bill 542
(Acts Ch. 112), unanimously in both chambers, requiring that agricultural value and
preexisting improvements such as fencing and water lines be counted in fair market value, and
barring false or misleading negotiation tactics by condemnors. The Commonwealth's policy
confirms that the losses described here are real and must be accounted for. The Commission
should give them weight in its own balancing.

 ISSUE 5: NO CONSTRUCTION ON A FARM BEFORE JUST COMPENSATION IS
                               PAID

A. The certificate is the source of the taking. The order states that the Commission has no
authority over compensation (PP 42, 46). But it is the Commission's certificate that gives
Columbia Gulf the power of eminent domain under 15 U.S.C. § 717f(h). The Commission




                                           Page 10 of 16
 cannot grant that power and then disclaim any responsibility for how it falls on the landowners
who bear it.

B. Without a condition, landowners carry the cost while the company waits. Once a
certificate is effective, federal courts have allowed pipeline companies to take immediate
possession of land through preliminary injunctions before compensation is determined. See
East Tennessee Natural Gas Co. v. Sage, 361 F.3d 808 (4th Cir. 2004). That leaves a farm
family carrying the costs of the company's project: the Padgetts are already paying, with
partial NRCS cost-share, for water and fencing the herd needs, while Columbia Gulf has not
said how it will meet its own watering commitment and has given no substantive answer to
their written proposals since July.

C. The Commission already conditions construction on prerequisites. The order bars
construction until Columbia Gulf files implementation plans, obtains written authorizations,
completes Endangered Species Act consultation, and completes cultural resource reviews
(Appendix, Conditions 6, 9, 13, 14). Requiring that, on each agricultural tract, Columbia Gulf
hold property rights acquired by agreement or have paid court-determined compensation
before construction begins there is the same kind of condition. It does not set any dollar
amount.

D. Farm families should not be made to finance a $413 million project. This is a $413
million project built for a single customer under a 20-year contract (Order P 5), on which
Columbia Gulf will earn a return. If its public benefits truly outweigh the harm to the farms in
its path, the project can bear the cost of paying those farms first. A project that can proceed
only by taking possession now and paying later has not shown that its benefits outweigh its
burdens on landowners, which is the balance the Certificate Policy Statement requires.

                                   RELIEF REQUESTED
Benjamin M. Padgett respectfully asks the Commission to:

   1. Grant rehearing of the October 15, 2026 order.
   2. Require East Kentucky Power Cooperative to state on the record whether any portion of
      the project's contracted capacity is intended to serve data-center or other large-load
      customers, including under confidentiality agreements, filed publicly or, at a minimum,
      under a protective agreement available to affected landowners.
   3. Reconsider its public convenience and necessity finding in light of that information, and
      explain how the project's public benefits outweigh the taking of agricultural land.




                                          Page 11 of 16
    4. Keep in place the stay of the certificate under Ordering Paragraph (B) while this request
      is pending, and deny any motion by Columbia Gulf to lift the stay unless it commits not
      to begin eminent domain proceedings against Tract KY-LI-066.000 before the
      Commission rules on this request.

Mr. Padgett further asks the Commission to clarify that Columbia Gulf's commitments to
provide livestock watering and to coordinate with breeding operations are binding under
Ordering Paragraph (A), and to add the following conditions to the certificate:

     Livestock water. Before ground disturbance on any affected tract, Columbia Gulf shall
     install permanent, frost-proof, automated livestock watering in every paddock separated
     from its water source by the right-of-way, operational at least 30 days before ground
     disturbance, and shall provide an equivalent dependable water supply to any
     confinement facility the landowner must use because paddocks are removed from
     service. Where a landowner has already installed such systems because Columbia Gulf
     did not act, Columbia Gulf shall file a statement identifying how it has satisfied its
     commitment on that tract before beginning construction there.
     Groundwater survey. At least 60 days before construction, Columbia Gulf shall
     complete and file a survey of wells, springs, and water lines on each affected
     agricultural tract.
     Breeding coordination. At least 90 days before construction, Columbia Gulf shall file a
     construction-scheduling plan, developed with each affected landowner, for active
     livestock breeding and calving operations within 500 yards of the project, including
     year-round calving herds. Where a year-round calving herd cannot be kept 500 yards
     from construction by scheduling alone, the plan shall provide a confinement facility,
     with its own dependable water supply, that keeps the cattle away from the construction
     site for the duration of construction and pasture recovery.
     Conservation practices. Before construction on any tract with practices installed under
     a USDA NRCS contract, Columbia Gulf shall consult with the landowner and NRCS,
